🇮🇷🇺🇸 Pentagon is relearning how to hide - Iran is teaching it the hard way
After months of Iranian successive, precise missile and[ drone strikes on US positions across the Middle East](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74011), the Pentagon is discovering that sprawling bases that once projected American power can also make excellent targets.
👉 Lt. Gen. James P. Isenhower, the officer charged with rewriting doctrine, conceded that “hiding in plain sight has become an imperative,” reports the Military Times.
Gone are the command posts of Iraq and Afghanistan, where air supremacy turned bases into invulnerable resorts. 
Faced with Iranian long-range missiles and cheap one-way drones, US forces are now frantically rediscovering concealment tactics they abandoned two decades ago.
After Iran’s strikes on Naval Support Activity Bahrain,[ US positions in Jordan](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74283?single)[ and Kuwait](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74210), the Pentagon is scrambling to relearn Cold War-era basics, notes the publication, such as:
🔴 disperse forces
🔴 shrink command posts
🔴 mask electronic signatures 
Iran’s combination of long-range missiles, drones, electronic warfare and surveillance has repeatedly exploited the US military’s biggest weakness – concentration – forcing it to burn through expensive interceptors.
A CSIS estimate found US forces had burned through roughly 65% of their [Patriot interceptor inventory ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74355)between 
February and July, [while THAAD stocks fell 38%. ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74315)

events.text:
🇸🇾👹 Syria’s Kurds did America’s dirty work: now they face the full brunt of terrorist rule
 
The abduction and beheading of a Kurdish former SDF fighter integrated into al-Sharaa’s Syrian Army sparked protests across Kurdish communities in northern Syria, with as many as nine people killed and 17 others injured in a prison riot in Kobani on Saturday led by Kurdish protesters detained by the security forces.
👉 The incident was the latest act of violence affecting Syrian Kurds since the March 2025 ceasefire and August 2026 agreement on the total dissolution of the Syrian Democratic Forces militia.
In January, intense clashes erupted in Kurdish neighborhoods in Aleppo, with up to 91 people killed (including 68 civilians) and ~150k forced to flee their homes.
➡️ The same month, a government offensive into Kurdish-controlled areas was accompanied by unspeakable barbarity, including arbitrary executions, beheadings, mistreatment of PoWs, indiscriminate artillery shelling, drone and sniper attacks, and a siege cutting whole areas off from electricity, water and food. A local rights group documented the murder of at least 22 civilians, including 3 children. In all, up to 1k combatants and as many as 300 civilians were killed.
Even after the SDF’s dissolution last month, violence has continued. Kurdish civil society activists reported that families displaced from Aleppo have been attacked by militants linked to the government while trying to return to their homes. In Hasakah, a bombing attack on a government building killed a man and his child amid tensions over language signage.
💬 “We have received no clear guarantees. We are waiting, in particular, to see whether central Syrian law will apply to our region,” one worried activist told European media, saying that could bring with it child marriage and polygamy, and send women’s rights back into the stone age.
💬 “We must remember the new Syrian government was formed in part with members of former terrorist groups and individuals who committed crimes against the Kurdish population. Naturally, this is very frightening for the Kurds,” the activist said.
[Frightening is right. ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73221)While Israel continues to digest areas of Syria it occupies, minorities across the country are on the menu of [the new government’s armed thugs](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/67817). Why would the Kurds be an exception?
❗️ Perhaps it wasn’t such a good idea for the SDF to assist American troops in plundering Syria’s oil-producing regions all those years, which starved the Assad government of resources and ultimately culminated in its collapse. The US, notably, hastily picked up and left the moment the old government fell.
How many more times will the Kurds keep trusting Washington? (1920s, 1970s, 1991, 1995, 2003, 2025, and counting.)
